newsitem.title: UK: British opposition attacks "Robert Maxwell" budget.
newsitem.headline: British opposition attacks "Robert Maxwell" budget.

text.p: Britain's opposition parties tried on Thursday to land their first telling blows on the new Labour government by claiming Wednesday's budget menaced the prosperity of every worker in the land when they reached retirement age.

Conservatives dubbed the budget of finance minister Gordon Brown "The Robert Maxwell Memorial Budget" after the business tycoon who left a 400 million pound black hole in the pension fund of his newspaper business when he died in 1991.
The National Association of Pension Funds was furious at a move by Brown to end a tax break under which funds could reclaim the tax paid on company dividends.

The move, which will raise 3.5 billion pounds ($5.9 billion) a year, was one of two major revenue-raising measures in the budget, the other being a windfall tax on excess profits made by privatised utilities, such as water and electricity companies.
"This is the biggest attack on pension funds since the (World) war (Two)," said the association's chairman, Peter Murray.
"This measure will take over 50 billion pounds of extra pension contributions from public and private sector employers over the next 10 years."

Peter Lilley, the new Conservative treasury spokesman, told journalists: "Companies as a whole will be worse off, and in the short term very much worse off, as they have to top up their pension funds."

Archie Kirkwood, social security spokesman for the minority Liberal Democrats, accused Brown of "sleight of hand" in introducing a measure of which, because of its complexity, many people would not see the implications.
"It would have been more honest to do it through the progressive introduction of income tax increases," he said.

Independent analysts saw Brown's move as politically astute, saying that although there would be an impact on companies, workers and current pensioners, it would be impossible for ordinary people to tell how much they had been affected.
"It is not going to be obvious to people that they are paying a tax," said Paul Johnson, deputy director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, a political think-tank.
"They are not going to notice. So the dissatisfaction may never filter through to the political level."

Alistair Darling, Brown's number two at the Treasury, dismissed the criticism, saying the tax system had been biased in favour of pension funds and that with a current surplus of 50 billion pounds in company funds, they were well placed to absorb the shock.

"I really have very little time for those who are critical of the changes that we have made. When they sit down and think about it, they will realise they will benefit pensioners as well as the country as a whole," he told a news conference.

The new government had already clashed with the pensions industry by tackling firms which it says sold membership of independent funds to 600,000 people who would have been better off staying with their company schemes.

It has demanded that the companies responsible fix strict deadlines for the compensation of victims of what Brown's junior minister Helen Liddell last month called "one of the worst scandals in financial services". ($ = 0.596 British Pounds)
